title: Practice Passage 7: The Search for Biosignatures on Exoplanets

passage.title: The Search for Biosignatures on Exoplanets
passage.sub_title: Analyzing how astronomers study exoplanetary atmospheres to identify chemical markers indicating alien life.
passage.content_html:
Section A
For centuries, the question of whether we are alone in the universe was the domain of philosophy and science fiction. However, over the past three decades, the field of astrobiology has transitioned into a rigorous observational science. The catalyst for this shift was the discovery of the first exoplanets—planets orbiting stars outside our solar system—in the early 1990s. Today, astronomers have confirmed the existence of thousands of exoplanets, ranging from massive gas giants to rocky worlds similar in size to Earth. The primary goal of modern astronomy has now shifted from merely finding these planets to determining whether any of them host life.

Section B
Since traveling to even the nearest exoplanet would take tens of thousands of years with current technology, astronomers must study them from immense distances. They do this by looking for 'biosignatures'—substances or phenomena that provide scientific evidence of past or present life. In the context of exoplanets, the most practical biosignatures are gases in the planet's atmosphere that can be detected using spectroscopy. When a planet passes in front of its host star, starlight filters through the atmosphere. By analyzing which wavelengths of light are absorbed by the gases, astronomers can identify the chemical composition of the atmosphere.

Section C
The search for atmospheric biosignatures focuses largely on finding chemical combinations that would not exist in equilibrium. On a dead planet, atmospheric gases reach a stable chemical state governed by geology and photochemistry. However, life disrupts this balance. The most famous example is the co-existence of oxygen and methane. Methane reacts quickly with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water. Therefore, if both oxygen and methane are found in large quantities in a planet's atmosphere, it suggests that both gases are being constantly replenished by active sources. On Earth, this replenishment is driven by photosynthesis (producing oxygen) and biological decay or digestion (producing methane).

Section D
However, identifying a potential biosignature is only the first step; astronomers must also rule out 'false positives'—abiotic processes that can mimic the chemical markers of life. For instance, oxygen can be produced without life if intense ultraviolet light breaks apart water vapor molecules in a planet's upper atmosphere, causing the lighter hydrogen to escape into space and leaving oxygen behind. Similarly, methane can be released through volcanic activity or chemical reactions in the planet's crust. To confirm a biosignature is biological, astronomers must evaluate the planet's overall environmental context, including its distance from the star and the star's activity level.

Section E
The search for alien life is entering an exciting new era with the launch of next-generation observatories. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched in late 2021, is already capturing high-resolution transmission spectra of exoplanet atmospheres. In the near future, ground-based mega-telescopes, such as the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) in Chile, will provide even greater capabilities. These advanced instruments will allow astronomers to analyze the atmospheres of Earth-sized planets situated within the 'habitable zone'—the orbital region where temperatures are mild enough to support liquid water. If life exists elsewhere in our galactic neighborhood, these telescopes may find the first evidence of it within our lifetimes.
